newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - High-tech companies battle for skilled employees.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - High-tech companies battle for skilled employees.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. hit the beach this year, setting up a tent near sunbathers at the Florida college spring break hot spot of Daytona Beach.
Company recruiters, dressed in shorts and sneakers, handed out IBM key chains and pens and invited graduating seniors to apply for jobs.

"I think there's more competition now for technical grads than there has been anytime in the past," said Dave Ferrell, manager of IBM's college recruiting. "There's a lot of talent running all over the place at the beach and we thought 'Hey, let's let them know about IBM.'"

High-technology companies, plagued with rising salaries and diminishing numbers of computer programmers and engineers, are looking for new ways to find and keep talented people in the fast-paced, ever-changing field.

The Internet craze spurred many companies to move into the high-technology field while the number of skilled newcomers has fallen. And industry sources said the battle for employees is intensifying as companies in all industries look for programmers to fix "Year 2000 bugs" in computer systems.
"We're going to enter a horrendous bidding war," Peter Mauro, a marketing representative manager for consulting firm C.W. Costello & Associates Inc., said at a course on Year 2000 solutions.

At a recent luncheon for Chicago business leaders, Motorola Inc. Chief Executive Christopher Galvin, when asked what keeps him awake at night, said: "Can we keep our team together. All of us (technology companies) have this problem."
In fact, Galvin said, Motorola begins recruiting future employees at age 14, through its summer camp and weekend technology programmes.

According to a study by the Information Technology Association of America released in February, the number of college students graduating with degrees in computer science fell by 43 percent to 24,200 in 1994 from 42,195 in 1986.

ITAA, which surveyed large- and mid-sized U.S. companies, found about 190,000 vacant information technology jobs nationwide, including one open position for every 10 information technology employees at tech-related companies.

Some 82 percent of the companies surveyed said they expected to expand their technology staff, while 68 percent cited a lack of skilled and trained workers as a barrier to their companies' future growth.

Many U.S. companies are looking outside the country for talent. U.S. Robotics Corp. Chief Executive Casey Cowell said his company purchased a Tel Aviv facility in part for the staff. 3Com Corp., which has agreed to buy U.S. Robotics, also purchased an Israeli company.

DePaul University of Chicago said its Student and Career Development Centre receives 150 calls and faxes a month from companies seeking to recruit graduates from the university's School of Computer Science, Telecommunications and Information Systems.
Starting salaries in the field currently range from $36,000 to $38,000, DePaul said, and students with master's degrees can expect up to $45,000 a year to start.

"Competition for people with computer expertise has increased so much that some companies are offering signing bonuses in addition to the attractive salary offers," said Joan Quinn, assistant director of the employment centre.

She said 60 percent to 70 percent of graduates are expected to have job offers by the time they graduate, and nearly 100 percent within six months of graduation. And some students even get offers midway through their study programmes.
Many companies turn to professional recruiters, some of whom reportedly have resorted on occasion to handing out business cards in parking lots of high-tech companies in Silicon Valley.

Jesus Bustamante, an electronic information specialist for the Web Design Group in Chicago, said he receives at least five calls a week from recruiters hoping to interest him in jobs across the country or to get the names of his friends in the industry.

Surprisingly, the battle for skilled employees has spurred some unlikely bedfellows. A consortium of some 14 companies make up the Talent Alliance, which among other things gives members access to each other's key workers for projects.
Members of the group include AT&T Corp., GTE Corp., Lucent Technologies Inc., NCR Corp. and Unisys Corp.
The companies intend to co-develop and share training programmes. The group has a job-matching web site that has helpful tips for job hunting and lists of available jobs.

"The high-tech industry had naturally some of the first companies to sign up, because of the shortage that they have in qualified talent," said Jeannette Galvanek, chief executive of Talent Alliance, herself on loan from AT&T.
